High above the valleys where the hardest fights took place, standing shoulder to shoulder with brothers in arms.   Delta Force A Squadron operator Lee Vampola, pictured on the far left, unfurls the American flag with his assault troop on a windswept ridgeline.   Born in 1985 and taken far too soon in 2024, Vampola belonged to the rarest breed of combat warriors. To earn a spot inside 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta demands surviving one of the most punishing, mentally exhausting selection courses known to the modern military. Men like Lee chose that fire willingly.   Look at the team dynamic captured in this mountain setting. Full MultiCam combat uniforms, low-profile ball caps, comms headsets rigged for immediate tactical communication, plate carriers, and dialed, suppressed assault carbines held at the ready. There are no theatrical poses or exaggerated stances here. Just a tight team of consummate professionals who lived in the dark, hunted the nation's most dangerous adversaries, and relied entirely on the operator to their left and right.   Operators inside Delta Force carry out hundreds of direct action raids and counter-terror strikes in complete anonymity. They do not seek fame or public applause. Their impact is measured by the missions completed, the lives shielded, and the brotherhood that holds firm long after the gear is packed away.Husband, father, and Tier 1 warrior who stood at the absolute tip of the spear.Lee Vampola.

This historic combat photograph captures former DEVGRU Red Squadron operator Rob O'Neill (bottom left, with blonde hair) administering IV fluids to exhausted U.S. Army Rangers during the intense search, rescue, and recovery operations following Operation Red Wings in the summer of 2005. 

Operating at high elevations in rugged Afghan terrain pushed even elite forces to their absolute physical limits. Severe dehydration, exhaustion, and relentless heat made basic medical maintenance like intravenous saline administration a daily necessity to keep teams combat-effective. 

During the massive manhunt and recovery mission for fallen Navy SEAL LT Michael Murphy and his reconnaissance team, Naval Special Warfare operators, Army Rangers, and support elements worked side-by-side in treacherous conditions to secure the mountains and bring their brothers home. 

Long before historical milestones or public acclaim, operators on the ground faced grueling, unglamorous days on the ridgelines—managing casualties, combat stress, and severe physical depletion under constant threat.

This rare look shows an Uruguayan military member holding an iconic, combat-proven M1A1 Thompson submachine gun—a weapon that first saw action on the battlefields of World War II over 80 years ago.   

Originally acquired through mid-20th-century U.S. military aid programs, the heavy, milled-steel M1A1 Thompson served as a frontline submachine gun in Uruguay until the mid-1980s, when it was officially replaced by the 9mm Argentine-made FMK-3 submachine gun. 

Rather than melting down or destroying obsolete small arms when new rifles arrive, the Uruguayan military has historically maintained a policy of preserving older weapons in deep-storage armories. Because of this, classic firearms like the M1A1 Thompson, M1 Garand, and M1 Carbine occasionally resurface for specialized familiarity training, reserve exercises, or ceremonial duties. 

Weighing in at roughly 10 pounds unloaded and firing the hard-hitting .45 ACP cartridge at 700+ rounds per minute, the simplified wartime M1A1 design is practically indestructible—proving that good steel and timeless engineering never truly go out of style.

CW4 Keith Yoakum, awarded Distinguished Service Cross, posthumous

Citation of Distinguished Service Cross, posthumous

CW4 Keith Yoakum,
Alpha Company, 1st Battalion, 227th Aviation Regiment
1st Air Cavalry Brigade, Multi-National Division (Baghdad)

CW4 Keith Yoakum distinguished himself by gallantry and courage at the risk of his own life above and beyond the call of duty as an AH-64D Longbow Apache Pilot-in Command while providing cover for his wingman on 2 February 2007 during aerial combat against a deliberate helicopter ambush site.

The previous two weeks in the Baghdad area of operations witnessed four separate attacks on coalition aircraft, resulting in the loss of 19 lives and the destruction of one AH-64D Longbow Apache, one UH-60 Blackhawk, and two Department of Defense contracted helicopters. CW4 Yoakum was the first responder to the UH-60 crash site and was intimately familiar with the enemy's helicopter ambush tactics.

CW4 Yoakum was the Pilot-in-Command of the trail aircraft in a flight of two AH-64D Longbow Apache helicopters as they departed on a reconnaissance mission in support of four separate ground brigades on the morning of 2 February 2007. Just when the Apache team began reconnaissance of a test fire area, waves of red tracers and heavy machine gun fire burst into the sky from multiple directions and raked the Apaches. The tracer fire immediately engulfed CW4 Yoakum's aircraft and riddled his fuselage. The enemy had established a deadly kill zone comprised of multiple heavy machine gun and anti-aircraft gun positions. With its interlocking fields of heavy anti-aircraft fire, the enemy ambush site was similar to the earlier ambush site that had downed a UH-60—the same UH-60 that CW4 Yoakum had responded to 13 days earlier, thus familiarizing him with the lethality of the enemy's tactics.

CW4 Yoakum immediately radioed his lead aircraft to maneuver it away from the direction of fire. As the lead aircraft broke hard to the right, the enemy responded, shifting its fire away from CW4 Yoakum's aircraft and toward the lead aircraft. CW4 Yoakum warned the lead helicopter announcing “now you're taking fire!” and the two aircraft broke left to escape the deadly kill zone.

Despite the damage to his aircraft, CW4 Yoakum took personal charge of the team amid the melee of bullets, calmed his lead aircraft, and steered the team out of the kill zone. The team raced to the north to separate from the enemy force and to acquire standoff range to assess the situation. Immediately after their turn to the north, CW4 Yoakum announced that he had “lost utility hydraulics,” a condition that requires the pilot to land the aircraft immediately at the nearest clear landing area. As the senior maintenance test pilot in the company, a prior instructor to other maintenance test pilots, and a Master Army Aviator with almost 5000 flight hours, CW4 Yoakum instantly understood the gravity of his Apache's emergency condition. Furthermore, CW4 Yoakum recognized that the loss of hydraulic pressure prevented him from employing his aircraft's main gun. As a result, he would have to use the aircraft's 2.75 inch rockets from a fixed position, requiring him to skillfully maneuver his crippled aircraft to accurately employ the rockets against the enemy.

The team continued northbound and after approximately two minutes no longer had tracers whipping by their windscreens. Once clear of the immediate threat, CW4 Yoakum had the opportunity to fly his critically damaged aircraft back to the airfield or land in the open desert to conduct an emergency extraction of his crew on his wingman's aircraft. He again announced “we've got no utility hydraulics left.” Still, despite the cockpit warnings and CW4 Yoakum's own recognition of his grave situation, he never considered leaving his wingman and knew this enemy would kill again if left on the battlefield. The enemy had a distinct advantage as a result of their concealed position among the numerous canals and irrigation ditches in the surrounding countryside. Despite the fierce danger inherent in pressing the attack, CW4 Yoakum radioed his wingman that “I can put rockets in” and continued to plan the route back into the withering fire of the enemy's ambush site to destroy the enemy's anti-aircraft positions.

CW4 Yoakum's instructions to his lead aircraft were simple: “you find them, we've got you covered.” CW4 Yoakum knew that his Apache team had a sliver of an opportunity to engage and destroy the enemy before they blended into the Iraqi countryside. The team decided to search the ambush area in a cloverleaf pattern, thereby performing a sweep of the area from all directions until they were able to locate the anti-aircraft guns. Despite his aircraft's crippled condition and the knowledge of the volume of fire that would again rake his aircraft at the ambush site, CW4 Yoakum was determined to cover his wingman as they searched for targets and eliminated the enemy position which was certain to be set up again at a different time and place to destroy coalition aircraft.

Approximately two minutes after the initial ambush had crippled CW4 Yoakum's Apache, the lead aircraft, acting on CW4 Yoakum's instructions, turned south to begin their search for the enemy ambush site. Despite the deteriorating condition of his own aircraft, CW4 Yoakum announced “I'm going to climb up and cover you from high and we're gonna work on rockets.” As he continued losing critical hydraulic pressure, CW4 Yoakum determined that his degraded weapons systems necessitated that he climb to altitude and then dive his damaged aircraft directly at the enemy to provide effective rocket fire. Only by diving from a higher altitude directly toward the enemy position could he provide precise rocket fire for his wingman while focusing his fires solely on the enemy and away from the surrounding villages and homes in the Iraqi countryside. With unmatched skill and extraordinary courage, CW4 Yoakum began his climb to posture his crippled aircraft in a diving position, knowing full well that his climb would give the enemy gunners a clearer line of sight and more time with which to engage his aircraft as he maneuvered back towards the ambush site.

CW4 Yoakum's focus on the destruction of the enemy's anti-aircraft guns caused him to demand as much from his aircraft as he did from himself, but his dying Apache was not able to sustain its altitude. As the Apache team made a second inbound run to the ambush area utilizing their cloverleaf pattern, the lead Apache radioed to CW4 Yoakum to ensure that he was still with them. After transmitting several radio calls and receiving no response, the lead aircraft began a left turn and acquired CW4 Yoakum's aircraft. After flying for almost four minutes in a critical state, CW4 Yoakum's Apache had succumbed to its battle damage and was engulfed in a blazing fire on the ground following a crash that had instantly killed CW4 Yoakum and his copilot.

CW4 Yoakum acted to protect his wingman and destroy an enemy anti-aircraft position designed to produce the continued loss of coalition aircraft. His decision to knowingly risk his life to cover his lead aircraft, despite having the opportunity to land or return to the airfield, put the accomplishment of his mission and the protection of his comrades over his own personal safety. His personal bravery and uncommon valor at the risk of his own life reflects great credit upon himself, the 1st Air Cavalry Brigade, the First Cavalry Division and the Multinational Division-Baghdad, and the United States Army.

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.

A comprehensive U.S. Army medical study examining the brutal physical toll of Ranger School has revealed that female soldiers who complete the course finish in better overall physiological condition than their male counterparts, experiencing significantly less hormonal disruption and preserving a higher percentage of lean muscle mass. 

Conducted by researchers from the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine (USARIEM) and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology and Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, the study tracked male and female candidates through the 61+ days of severe caloric deprivation, minimal sleep, and non-stop physical exertion across the Darby, Mountain, and Swamp phases. 

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Men lost significantly more total body mass and lean muscle tissue, whereas female candidates metabolized fat stores more efficiently—preserving their fat-free muscle mass to a much greater extent and exhibiting fewer extreme drops in metabolic and endocrine hormone markers. 

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. It doesn't matter what your sex is."

Can a dedicated 26-Marine Scout Platoon fully replace the legendary Scout Sniper platoons and give infantry commanders the ultimate eyes and ears on the modern battlefield? 

The U.S. Marine Corps’ newest primary infantry career field—the 0315 Marine Scout—is officially in effect, establishing a dedicated reconnaissance and surveillance pipeline on the heels of the Corps' controversial decision to phase out traditional Scout Sniper platoons in 2023.   

Previously treated as an additional skillset rather than a standalone career path, Marine Scouts now hold their own Primary Military Occupational Specialty (PMOS 0315) alongside riflemen (0311), machine gunners (0331), and mortarmen (0341). 

These specially trained Marines populate a 26-Marine Scout Platoon inside each infantry battalion—as well as scout teams within Light Armored Reconnaissance (LAR) battalions. Each scout team also embeds a certified Joint Fires Observer (JFO) capable of calling in devastating air and artillery strikes on high-value enemy targets. 

Trained in advanced fieldcraft, stealth, unmanned aerial systems, and assured long-range communications, 0315 Scouts are built to slip ahead of the main force, map routes to the objective, and extend an infantry battalion's sensing capabilities across contested littoral and inland environments.

Should mandatory "religious liberty training" and expanded roles for chaplains be implemented across the entire U.S. military?   

U.S. service members and commanders could soon be required to complete annual "religious liberty training" following sweeping recommendations from a White House-directed commission aimed at expanding faith-based protections across the armed forces.   

Chaired by Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and former cabinet secretary Ben Carson, the federal Religious Liberty Commission issued a comprehensive report urging the Pentagon to implement annual training on religious accommodations, protect personal religious expression in the ranks, and integrate "religious liberty impact assessments" into operational planning. 

The panel also called on the military to produce an updated "spiritual fitness guide" and elevate the role of military chaplains—building on recent Pentagon moves to establish an Office of Religious Affairs and restore troops who previously sought religious exemptions from vaccine mandates. 

While Pentagon officials stated they welcome the recommendations as a vital step toward protecting First Amendment conscience rights for those in uniform, critics and some service members argue that adding another mandatory annual training block could spark debate over how different faiths are represented across a diverse force.

Cody Alford lived at the sharp end of the spear. He deployed on multiple combat tours to Iraq and Afghanistan, leading sniper teams, kicking doors, and surviving under relentless enemy fire.

He earned the Bronze Star with Valor. But the battlefield takes a toll that body armor can't stop.

Hundreds of close-range breaching blasts, artillery concussions, and IED shockwaves tore through his brain. By the end of his career, Cody was suffering from severe Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), neurological breakdown, vestibular failure, and crippling PTSD.

His body and mind were shutting down.

When the uniform came off, the silence was louder than gunfire. Cody found himself stripped of his identity, struggling through neurological fog, and fighting just to function each day.

But instead of surrendering to the spiral, Cody chose to wage a new war—the war for his own mind and life.

Through intense neuro-rehabilitation, discipline, and honest self-examination, he rebuilt himself from the inside out.

He shared his entire journey on The Shawn Ryan Show, giving millions of veterans permission to acknowledge their invisible combat injuries and seek real healing. Today, through his platform We Are The They, he mentors people to break through mental barriers and conquer their internal battles.

The scars you can't see are often the hardest to heal.

The U.S. Navy is officially ushering in the era of autonomous naval warfare.

In a historic first, the USS Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group has deployed to the Pacific accompanied by an autonomous Medium Unmanned Surface Vessel (MUSV)—integrating robotic drone warships directly into strike group combat operations.

Senior naval leadership confirmed this week that the fleet is pushing for a far more visible, aggressive operational role for unmanned surface vessels:

Forward Sensor Pickets: Sailing hundreds of miles ahead of the carrier to detect enemy submarines, warships, and low-flying anti-ship cruise missiles without risking human lives.

Electronic Warfare & Decoy Nodes: Emitting false radar signatures and jamming enemy targeting networks to draw hostile fire away from manned destroyers and aircraft carriers.

Distributed Lethality: Preparing for future swarm configurations where armed unmanned boats can launch precision strikes deep inside contested anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) missile bubbles.

As near-peer adversaries expand long-range ballistic missile capabilities and cheap one-way drone swarm tactics, the Navy is betting heavily on unmanned autonomy to maintain freedom of navigation in the Pacific.

Naval warfare is transforming before our eyes.

Are unmanned drone warships the future of maritime dominance, or can robotic systems never truly replace manned warships and combat-hardened sailors?

HARRILL, JOHN D., III, SILVER STAR RECIPIENT

Citation: The President of the United States takes pleasure in presenting the Silver Star Medal to John D. Harrill, III, Major, U.S. Marine Corps, for conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity in action against the enemy while serving as Operations Officer, Second Battalion, Fourth Marine Regiment, FIRST Marine Division, I Marine Expeditionary Force, U.S. Marine Corps Forces, Central command, in support of Operation IRAQI FREEDOM from February to September 2004. Major Harrill's leadership and heroism while under fire contributed materially to the battalion's success in preventing the fall of Ar Ramadi, Iraq. Throughout enemy attacks and offensive operations, he calmly led the battalion command element and coordinated maneuver of the battalion's combat units, while personally neutralizing enemy automatic weapon and rocket-propelled grenade fire, resulting in the enemy's defeat. During a major insurgent attack against coalition forces, Major Harrill led the forward command element into the aim point of the enemy attack. Despite constant enemy fire, he focused the combat power of six companies as they battled in eight separate locations over a seven-hour period. Major Harrill's superior tactical acumen enabled the complete destruction of assaulting enemy forces. By his bold leadership, courageous actions, and loyal devotion to duty, Major Harrill reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the Marine Corps and the United States Naval Service.

The U.S. Army has officially issued a major policy directive (MILPER 26-350) granting automatic promotion to Staff Sergeant (E-6) for any Sergeant (E-5) who successfully completes and graduates from the U.S. Army Drill Sergeant Academy.

The policy also applies retroactively to eligible sergeants currently serving on the trail.

The move bumps new instructors from the E-5 to E-6 pay grade—delivering an immediate base pay raise of roughly $3,000+ per year, in addition to Special Duty Assignment Pay (SDAP) and immediate seniority when leading initial entry trainees.

The Pentagon's objective is clear: incentivize high-performing NCOs to volunteer for the trail to fix critical staffing shortages at Basic Combat Training installations like Fort Moore, Fort Jackson, Fort Leonard Wood, and Fort Sill.

Being on the trail is one of the most grueling assignments in the military—facing 60-to-80-hour workweeks, waking up at 04:00, and bearing the heavy responsibility of transforming civilians into disciplined soldiers.

But within the ranks, the move has reignited a fierce debate:

Supporters argue this is well-earned recognition for taking on one of the most stressful, burnout-heavy duties in the armed forces.

Critics argue that automatic promotions bypass traditional cutoff points and boards, allowing soldiers to skip competitive requirements ahead of peers in operational units.

Is an automatic stripe a fair reward for surviving the trail, or does it undermine the traditional promotion system?

BREAKING: Legendary British actor Sir Patrick Stewart has passed away at the age of 86.

Across a masterclass career spanning more than six decades, Stewart brought an unmatched Shakespearean dignity, commanding presence, and deep moral weight to every character he inhabited:

Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Star Trek: Picard—teaching generations the true meaning of duty, diplomacy, and principled leadership.

Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise and Logan—the intellectual and moral anchor of superhero cinema.

Decades of Classical Theatre: A pillar of the Royal Shakespeare Company, commanding stages across London, Broadway, and around the world.

Knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for services to drama, Stewart was also a passionate advocate for domestic violence awareness and veterans' trauma, inspired by his own father’s struggles with severe combat PTSD following World War II.

Whether seated in the captain's chair of the USS Enterprise or leading the X-Men, Sir Patrick Stewart embodied strength through wisdom, compassion, and unwavering conviction.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has issued an explicit, direct warning to the United States and NATO: Russia is "prepared for war," and if tensions cross the point of no return, "there will be no winners."

Speaking during a state address in Moscow, Putin directly addressed escalating Western defense commitments, long-range precision missile approvals, and expanding intelligence coordination on the European continent:

Direct Clash Warning: Putin warned that expanding Western involvement risks crossing into an overt military conflict between nuclear-armed superpowers.

No Winners in a Major War: Emphasizing Russia's upgraded strategic and non-strategic nuclear doctrine, Putin reminded Western capitals that any direct clash with NATO would rapidly escalate beyond conventional limits.

Readiness Posture: Signaling that Russian military forces, hypersonic strike systems, and strategic nuclear triads remain on continuous high-alert status.

The stark warning comes at a critical juncture:

NATO leaders maintain that unwavering strength, collective defense, and deterrence are the only ways to prevent further aggression.

Geopolitical realists and defense analysts warn that continuing to climb the escalation ladder without an off-ramp risks sleepwalking into an catastrophic confrontation where miscalculation triggers a third world war.

As rhetoric sharpens and red lines blur, the world is watching the most dangerous geopolitical standoff since the Cuban Missile Crisis.

Is Putin's statement a desperate bluff to freeze Western support, or is the world inching closer to an uncontrollable direct confrontation?

For the first time since the Korean War, the U.S. Army is actively preparing for the grimmest reality of large-scale combat: digging temporary mass graves directly on the battlefield.

During recent high-intensity readiness exercises at Fort Liberty, North Carolina, combat engineers from the 20th Engineer Brigade, soldiers from the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, mortuary affairs specialists, and Army chaplains trained with heavy bulldozers and excavators to establish standardized field burial sites.

The metrics from the exercise are chilling:

Standardized burial trenches for 20 fallen soldiers can be excavated in just 75 minutes.

Using eight bulldozers and four military excavators, an engineering unit could temporarily inter the remains of up to 2,400 soldiers within a single 24-hour window.

For the past 20 years in Iraq and Afghanistan, the U.S. military enjoyed complete air dominance. Every fallen warrior was treated with reverent custody and flown directly home to Dover Air Force Base within days.

But Pentagon war games for a potential clash against a near-peer adversary—such as China or Russia—reveal a brutal reality:

Contested airspace, anti-ship missiles, and cyber-disrupted logistics could sever supply lines for weeks.

Immediate air repatriation would be physically impossible, and casualty counts could reach thousands in days.

Frontline units would be forced to temporarily inter fallen soldiers in the dirt to maintain positive identification, prevent disease, and protect remains until the combat zone can be secured for repatriation.

As Sergeant 1st Class Delbert Ruede stated during the drills: "If we went to war tomorrow, we would be making this up as we went along. What we are doing here is taking a scientific, field-tested approach so that we can maintain positive control and respectfully care for our fallen."

Practicing the unthinkable is the starkest sign yet of how seriously military planners view the threat of major war.

Is the military being responsibly realistic about near-peer warfare, or is this a chilling warning of where global tensions are heading?

The Pentagon, U.S. Army Criminal Investigation Division (CID), and U.S. Cyber Command are officially investigating a wave of simultaneous, catastrophic freezer meltdowns across military base commissaries as a suspected foreign cyberattack.

In recent weeks, commercial refrigeration systems at commissaries across multiple major military installations including Fort Huachuca and bases across several states inexplicably malfunctioned at the exact same time. The sudden temperature overrides thawed massive freezer rows, spoiling hundreds of thousands of dollars in groceries and leaving military families with empty shelves.

Federal investigators quickly connected the dots: the incident closely mirrors a sophisticated cyberattack in France that remotely hacked and shut down environmental cooling controls across more than 350 commercial supermarkets.

While spoiled commissary food might sound like an annoyance on the surface, cybersecurity and military intelligence analysts warn that this is a classic asymmetric infrastructure probe:

Operational Technology (OT) Infiltration: Hostile nation-state hacking groups (such as China or Russia) are actively testing their ability to breach the industrial control systems and software running U.S. military installations.

The Wartime Threat: If foreign hackers can remotely shut down cooling systems in base grocery stores, the exact same networked SCADA vulnerabilities can be used during a conflict to overheat classified supercomputer data centers, ruin temperature-sensitive missile propellant in munitions depots, and destroy military medical blood and vaccine banks.

Gray-zone cyber warfare isn't coming in the future—it's already hitting domestic bases inside our own borders.

Is targeting grocery stores and base infrastructure an early warning of a massive cyber conflict, or are military networks too vulnerable to basic commercial hacking?

BREAKING: Israel has reportedly submitted plans to Washington requesting U.S. approval and operational coordination to conduct targeted military strikes against Iranian energy and oil infrastructure.

According to regional intelligence reports, the proposed strike packages focus on crippling key Iranian economic lifelines:

Strategic Crude Export Terminals: Including vital export hubs like Kharg Island, which handles over 90% of Iran's seaborne petroleum exports.

Domestic Refining & Storage Facilities: Targeting state-run refineries to disrupt internal fuel supplies and logistics used by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Power & Energy Grid Nodes: Disabling primary electrical generation stations powering critical defense installations and drone manufacturing sites.

The reported request puts Washington in a high-stakes geopolitical crossroad:

Proponents argue that taking out Iran's energy revenues is the single most effective non-nuclear measure to permanently starve Tehran's proxy networks and ballistic missile programs.

Critics and energy analysts warn that striking major Iranian oil infrastructure could trigger an immediate spike in global crude prices and provoke direct ballistic counter-strikes against Gulf energy infrastructure and international shipping lanes.

With tensions at a boiling point across the Middle East, all eyes are on Washington’s response.

Should the U.S. green-light strikes on Iran's energy infrastructure to cripple its military funding, or would targeting oil hubs ignite a wider economic and military catastrophe?

Major Jeffrey R. Calero was an elite Special Forces detachment commander with Company C, 1st Battalion, 20th Special Forces Group (Airborne).

Originally from Puerto Rico and raised in New York, Calero was brilliant and driven. He earned his mechanical engineering degree from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) before choosing a life of service, earning his Green Beret in 2001.

As an officer, Calero believed in leading from the front. He never asked his men to take a step he wouldn't take first.

On October 29, 2007, while leading an Operational Detachment Alpha (ODA 2132) on a high-risk dismounted combat patrol through hostile terrain in Kajaki, an improvised explosive device (IED) was triggered.

Major Calero was killed in action, giving his life in defense of his team and his country. He was 34 years old.

Awarded the Bronze Star Medal and Purple Heart, Major Calero represented the highest standard of leadership, quiet professionalism, and selfless sacrifice within the Special Forces brotherhood.

A leader walks ahead of his men. A hero lives on in their hearts forever.

Strict liberty crackdowns and curfews have hit American service members stationed in Japan.

Following the arrest of an American service member for the alleged murder of a local woman in Okinawa, military leadership at Kadena Air Base has enacted immediate, sweeping restrictions targeting junior enlisted personnel (E-1 through E-4).

The new order clamps down hard on junior troops across the installation:

Total Alcohol Prohibition: A complete ban on purchasing or consuming alcohol, both on-base and off-base.

Mandatory Curfew: Strict nighttime curfews requiring junior enlisted airmen to remain inside their residences or barracks.

Restricted Off-Base Liberty: Heightened accountability checks and travel limits across the island.

The incident has reignited long-standing geopolitical tensions between the local Okinawan government and the Pentagon regarding the heavy U.S. military footprint on the island.

But within the ranks, the move has triggered a familiar, heated debate over collective punishment:

Supporters argue that leadership must take immediate, drastic measures to de-escalate host-nation outrage, prevent further incidents, and preserve critical bilateral defense alliances in the Pacific.

Critics and junior enlisted troops argue that punishing thousands of disciplined, law-abiding service members for the egregious criminal actions of one individual destroys morale and fails to solve the underlying problem.

Anyone who has been stationed overseas knows this drill all too well.

Is blanket punishment on junior enlisted troops necessary to manage diplomatic fallout, or is it an outdated leadership tactic that punishes the wrong people?

Nineteen Choctaw men are remembered as the first code talkers — the pioneers whose idea the Navajo, Comanche and two dozen other tribes would carry into the next war. Before there were hundreds, there were twenty-nine. 🇺🇸

In May 1942, twenty-nine young Navajo men — shepherds, students, farmers' sons — walked into Marine boot camp as the first all-Navajo platoon in Corps history. At Camp Elliott in San Diego, they were locked into classrooms with a top-secret order: invent an unbreakable code, from scratch, in their own language.

Working day and night, the 29 built it in layers — a phonetic alphabet (A for "ant," B for "bear") and a dictionary of military terms that grew past 400 words, every one of them memorized, because nothing could ever be written down in the field. In testing, they encoded, sent and decoded a three-line message in twenty seconds. The Marines' best machines took thirty minutes.

Their code went to war across the Pacific and was never broken — the only oral code in modern military history that never fell. By 1945 more than 400 Navajo code talkers were serving, and at Iwo Jima their six networks handled more than 800 messages in the first two days without a single error. Their commanding signal officer said it plainly: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima."

In 2001, the surviving members of the Original 29 received the Congressional Gold Medal. The bronze talker on his knees at Window Rock, radio in hand, stands for all of them — twenty-nine young men who turned the language of home into a shield for a nation.

He had spent his last days fighting to bring his soldiers home — and more than six decades later, his country finally brought him home.

On a little hill in Pennsylvania, a professor gave an order that saved the Union — and his little brother stood beside him. 🇺🇸

Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain, pictured here, was a Bowdoin College professor of rhetoric who spoke ten languages and had no military training when he talked his way into the Army. By July 2, 1863, he commanded the 20th Maine — and held the extreme left end of the entire Union line on Little Round Top at Gettysburg, with orders to hold "to the last." Among the officers beside him was his younger brother, Lieutenant Thomas Chamberlain.

All afternoon the 20th Maine beat back wave after wave of Alabamians climbing the rocks. Then the ammunition ran out. What Joshua did next is studied in war colleges to this day: he fixed bayonets and ordered a downhill charge — the line swinging like a gate — that swept the stunned Confederates off the hill and, many historians believe, saved the Army of the Potomac. He was wounded so often in that war that newspapers printed his obituary by mistake; Grant chose him to formally receive the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, where Chamberlain ordered his men to salute their defeated enemies as they stacked their arms.

Thomas did not live to see the peace — disease, the silent k*ller of every Civil War camp, claimed him in 1864. Joshua carried his brother's memory through fifty more years: governor, college president, and the old soldier whose name still means Little Round Top.

Can modern forensic breakthroughs finally bring closure to families more than five decades after one of America's most notorious serial killers struck?

Summit County, Utah prosecutors and law enforcement officials have formally linked infamous serial killer Ted Bundy to the unsolved October 1974 murder of 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith through advanced DNA testing.

A 52-Year Cold Case Solved: Melissa Ann Smith disappeared in late October 1974, and her body was later discovered in Summit County by hunters. For decades, her murder remained officially unsolved despite long-standing suspicions regarding Bundy's presence in Utah while attending law school.

The Forensics Breakthrough: Investigators closed the case after connecting genetic evidence preserved from Smith's autopsy to DNA profiles established in the case of Laura Aime—another 17-year-old Utah victim whose murder was definitively tied to Bundy through DNA earlier this year.

Closing the Book on Unsolved Victims: Executed in Florida's electric chair in 1989, Bundy confessed to dozens of killings across Washington, Utah, Colorado, Idaho, and Florida, though several remained unconfirmed. Utah investigators emphasized that every cold case closure helps bring answers to surviving families while bringing permanent resolution to his trail of crimes.

Two brothers of one Wisconsin family — and between them, two of the Civil War's most impossible feats. 🇺🇸

Alonzo Cushing, pictured here, was a 22-year-old artillery lieutenant whose battery stood at the very center of the Union line at Gettysburg — the stone wall called the Angle — on July 3, 1863. As Pickett's Charge rolled toward him, Alonzo was wounded again and again: a shell fragment through the shoulder, another through the body. Ordered to the rear, he refused, had himself held upright beside his last serviceable gun, and was sighting it with his thumb over the vent when a bullet struck him down at his post. The charge broke on the ground he would not leave. In November 2014 — 151 years later — President Barack Obama placed Alonzo Cushing's Medal of Honor where it had always belonged.

His younger brother needed no land battle for his legend. William Barker Cushing of the U.S. Navy, on the night of October 27, 1864, steamed a tiny launch with a spar torpedo up the dark Roanoke River, alone past Confederate guards, and detonated it beneath the ironclad CSS Albemarle — sinking the South's most feared warship and swimming for his life through icy water as it went down.

One brother held the line at the war's turning point. The other sank an ironclad in the dark. America has rarely asked more of one family's sons — and never received more.

One family. Six months. Four telegrams. 🇺🇸

Alben and Gunda Borgstrom, a farming couple from Thatcher, Utah, sent their sons to war one after another. In 1944, the telegrams began to arrive — and they did not stop.

First came word of Clyde, a Marine on Guadalcanal, lost in March 1944. Then LeRoy, a soldier, gone in the fighting in the summer of 1944. Then Rolon, lost in France. Then Rulon, an airman, missing over Europe and declared d*ad. Four brothers, lost within six months — in the Pacific and in Europe, on the sea of war's every front — while their parents kept the farm and their faith and waited for news of the boys who remained.

What was left of the family's strength, the military itself moved to protect: their fifth serving son, Boyd, was ordered home out of harm's way, released from further combat service so the Borgstrom line would not be extinguished entirely — one of the cases that hardened America's resolve to protect sole surviving sons.

In June 1948, the Army brought the four brothers home together. Thousands gathered in Utah as Clyde, LeRoy, Rolon and Rulon were laid to rest side by side in the Thatcher cemetery — four white markers, one unbearable row, and a nation's debt written in a single family's names.

FORT BENNING, Ga. (USASOC News Service, Dec. 2, 2009) -- A squad leader with the 75th Ranger Regiment was awarded the Silver Star for risking his life to save two fellow Rangers in Afghanistan.

"Any Ranger would have done the same thing," said Staff Sgt. Michael E. Norton of Alpha Company, 3rd Battalion, 75th Rangers. "The Ranger Creed says, 'I will never leave a fallen comrade.' There was no moment of thinking about what to do. I had to get my brothers, and the most important thing in my mind was how hurt they were."

Norton led his squad on an objective, Aug. 4-5, to raid an enemy combatant's headquarters camp in the mountains of northwestern Khowst Province in Afghanistan.

While moving to the objective, Norton and one of his team leaders were alerted to possible enemy combatants along the route and moved forward to assess the situation. As Norton and his team leader were attempting to identify the possible enemy in the valley, a seven—to nine-man enemy element initiated a complex, near ambush on Norton's squad from the high ground with rocket-propelled grenades and small arms fire from a position 25 meters to the squad's front.
"The fire came from our 12 o'clock and then maybe a couple of seconds later from our right and left," Norton said.

Behind the first enemy rocket-propelled grenade team, a medium machine gun on elevated ground to the northwest engaged them with highly effective fire. Two more enemy combatants were on the slope of the valley to the west, engaged the Ranger squad with an AK-47 and rocket-propelled grenades along the long axis of their formation, while another group of enemy fighters were on elevated terrain to the east, raked them with small arms fire from the rear of the Ranger squad formation.

The multiple enemy positions had effectively enveloped Norton's squad from multiple directions at a distance of 25 to 50 meters, leaving Norton and his element pinned to the floor of the valley by the intense and accurate small arms fire.

The valley left no room for maneuver; Norton, his squad and the machine gun team element behind them immediately returned fire, but they were unable to gain fire superiority over the well-established enemy.

After the second rocket-propelled grenades knocked two of his Rangers temporarily unconscious and blasted the rest of his squad with shrapnel and debris and realizing his element could not gain fire superiority, Norton shouted for his squad to break contact.

When Norton realized that two Rangers had not gotten up and were still exposed to the heavy volume of enemy fire from the high ground to the east and west, and with complete disregard for his own safety, Norton turned around and with marked distinction, purposefully charged back into the interlocking fire of the enemy ambush kill zone in order to recover his downed Rangers.

"The example of personal courage that Staff Sergeant Norton showed, to get his men out of the kill zone is a testament to his character," said Maj. Keith Carter, A Company commander. "NCOs such as Staff Sergeant Norton are the reason I wanted to serve in the 75th Ranger Regiment, and it is an honor to lead them."

Without hesitation, Norton dove down into the midst of enemy fire with his unconscious comrades, uncertain of their status.

"There was nothing fancy going on in my head besides hoping they weren't dead," said Norton.

While the rest of the element attempted to suppress the enemy, and lying next to the Rangers, Norton "started shaking and yelling as quietly as I could."

After reviving his Rangers, Norton led them back to cover through the hail of direct fire and rocket-propelled grenade strikes, saving their lives and bringing his entire squad out of the enemy onslaught intact.

"I'm proud of the actions of my squad, because we continued the mission after that," said Norton. "It was just two minutes out of our overall mission."

As his platoon fought off the enemy ambush with direct fire, mortars and close air support, Norton quickly assessed his casualties and reorganized his squad to return to the fight.

Norton continued leading his squad in the follow-on assaults through two more direct fire contacts, killing two enemy combatants.

"We receive a lot of great training here at 3rd Ranger Battalion and I was just acting on instinct," said Norton.

The training conducted by Rangers means everything on the battlefield.

"The goal of the company and battalion is to create the most realistic scenarios possible while minimizing risk," Carter said. We constantly integrate new enemy tactics from overseas into our training so that we are ready in any situation."

The overall assault force killed 20 enemy fighters and destroyed two enemy anti-aircraft guns and several other weapons, explosives, and military supplies on the objective, disrupting a major enemy headquarters and encampment.

Norton joined the Army from his hometown of Pensacola, Fla., June 2004, after graduating from West Highland Christian Academy, and has deployed six times in support of operations Enduring and Iraqi Freedom. He is the son of Jimmy and Deborah Norton of Holly, Mich.

This is the true story behind Saving Private Ryan — and the truth is harder than the film. 🇺🇸

Four brothers from Tonawanda, New York, went to war: Edward, Preston, Robert and Frederick "Fritz" Niland. In one terrible June of 1944, the family's world collapsed. Robert, a paratrooper of the 82nd Airborne, was k*lled on D-Day itself at Neuville-au-Plain. The very next day, June 7, Preston, also a paratrooper, fell near Utah Beach. And from the other side of the world came word that Edward, an airman whose plane had gone down in the Burmese jungle, was missing and presumed d*ad.

That left Fritz, fighting with the 101st Airborne in Normandy. When the Army realized three brothers were gone, it moved fast: the regimental chaplain, Father Francis Sampson, tracked Fritz down and the last Niland son was pulled from the line and sent home to his mother — the real "sole survivor" mission that Steven Spielberg later transformed into Saving Private Ryan.

And then, in 1945, came the telegram no one dared hope for: Edward was alive. Emaciated in a Japanese prison camp, he had survived. Two Niland brothers came home. Two rest side by side today in the American cemetery above Normandy — Preston and Robert, together, under white crosses in Plot B.

Five brothers. One ship. One night that changed America's rules of war forever. 🇺🇸

George, Francis, Joseph, Madison and Albert Sullivan were five Irish-American brothers from Waterloo, Iowa. When their friend Bill Ball was k*lled aboard the USS Arizona at Pearl Harbor, the brothers enlisted together — with one condition the Navy granted: they would serve together. All five were posted to the light cruiser USS Juneau, and their smiling photograph aboard her became one of the famous images of the young war.

On the night of November 13, 1942, in the savage naval battles off Guadalcanal, a Japanese torpedo struck the Juneau's magazine. She disintegrated and sank in less than a minute. Some hundred men survived the sinking and clung to rafts in shark-haunted water — but through a chain of communication failures, no rescue came for days. When help finally arrived, only ten men were pulled out alive. All five Sullivan brothers were gone.

Their mother Alleta received the news with a grace that humbled a nation, and their sister Genevieve joined the Navy's WAVES in their honor. The Navy named a destroyer USS The Sullivans — the only American warship ever named for a family — and the tragedy drove the military to separate siblings and protect sole surviving sons. "We stick together" was the brothers' motto. They did — to the very end.
